# Geothermal wells: how deep they go, what they cost and how long they last.

Geothermal power wells reach 1.5 to 2.5 kilometres for a typical conventional plant and 3 to 7 kilometres for deep enhanced geothermal, by the national laboratories' cost baseline. Drilling one costs millions of dollars: Fervo Energy's Cape Station wells fell from $9.4 million to $4.8 million each. They produce for decades, while the water they bring up slowly cools; in Nevada's public record the median field ran about 1.9 °F cooler each year.

Drilling figures come from the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR, formerly NREL) and company statements, labelled as such. Field temperatures are measured and operator-reported to the Nevada Division of Minerals; yearly rates are computed by Zemanium from that record.

01 / In brief

## Geothermal wells at a glance.

- Depth: NLR's representative conventional plants draw on 175 °C water at 1.5 km and 225 °C water at 2.5 km; deep enhanced geothermal targets 3 to 7 km. The EIA notes some geothermal wells reach about 2 miles.
- Cost: drilling makes up 30% to 57% of a new plant's capital cost. Fervo's Cape Station wells cost $346 to $634 per foot drilled, against $995 and $1,107 at its Project Red pilot.
- Speed: the fastest of the first six Cape Station wells took 20 days for 13,289 feet. Fervo reported 19,448 feet in 21 days at its Sawtooth 7 well in 2026.
- Life: NLR's cost baseline assumes 30 years for plant and reservoir. The Geysers in California has produced power since 1960.
- Cooling: in 11 of 18 long-running Nevada fields the produced water is more than 5 °F cooler than in its first recorded year.

02 / Depth

## How deep are geothermal wells?

As deep as the heat requires. Geothermal power plants need water or steam at 300 to 700 °F, according to the EIA, and how far down that sits depends on the local geology. Recent wells with public records:

| Well | Measured depth | Temperature | Drilling time | Basis |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GDC-36, The Geysers, California (2023) | 9,000 ft (2,743 m) | steam above 475 °F (246 °C) | 69 days | NLR 2025 |
| Project Red pair, Nevada | 11,211 and 11,220 ft (3.42 km) | 376 °F (191 °C) maximum | 59 and 72 days | NLR 2025 |
| Utah FORGE 16B(78)-32 (2023) | 10,947 ft (3.34 km) | research site | 75 days | NLR 2025 |
| Cape Station, Utah, 14 horizontal wells (2023 to 2024) | 13,272 to 15,347 ft (4.0 to 4.7 km), laterals about 4,700 ft | 444 °F (229 °C) maximum | 20 to 34 days for the first six | NLR 2025 |
| Sawtooth 7, Utah (2026) | 19,448 ft (5.9 km) with a 7,500 ft lateral | about 238 °C rock | 21 days | company statement |
| IDDP-2, Reykjanes, Iceland | logged at about 4,550 m | 426 °C | research well | World Geothermal Congress paper |

Measured depth is the length of the hole. Horizontal wells such as Cape Station's run sideways for thousands of feet at their target, so their vertical depth is shorter than their measured depth.

03 / Cost

## How much does it cost to drill a geothermal well?

Millions of dollars per well, and falling. NLR's 2025 analysis of Fervo's wells, using data Fervo supplied:

| Well | Total depth | Days | Feet per day | Cost per foot |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Project Red 1 | 11,220 ft | 71 | 158 | $994.62 |
| Project Red 2 | 11,211 ft | 58 | 193 | $1,106.74 |
| Cape Station 3 | 13,316 ft | 33.75 | 312 | $633.45 |
| Cape Station 4 | 13,272 ft | 25.91 | 440 | $471.59 |
| Cape Station 5 | 13,601 ft | 24.26 | 504 | $395.71 |
| Cape Station 6 | 13,289 ft | 20.1 | 567 | $346.45 |
| Cape Station 7 | 13,949 ft | 23.71 | 472 | $394.08 |
| Cape Station 8 | 13,734 ft | 22.27 | 539 | $357.36 |

At $346.45 a foot, Cape Station 6 cost about $4.6 million to drill, before completion. Fervo itself reported its Cape Station well cost falling from $9.4 million to $4.8 million. NLR attributes the gains to diamond (PDC) bits, drilling practices that remove the limits on speed one by one, and drilling several wells from one pad, and its 2025 cost curves sit 12% to 24% below the 2017 baseline for vertical wells and 18% to 26% below for horizontal ones.

Casing and cementing alone make up 30% to 40% or more of a well's cost, according to the US Department of Energy. And not every well finds what it is drilled for: NLR's baseline assumes 60% of exploration wells at a new conventional site succeed.

What well costs do to the price of power is in our [cost guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-electricity-cost), and the [LCOE calculator](https://zemanium.com/lcoe-calculator) turns any capital cost into dollars per megawatt-hour.

04 / Lifespan

## How long do geothermal wells last?

Decades. NLR's cost baseline assumes a 30-year life for plant and reservoir, and The Geysers in California has produced electricity since 1960, according to the EIA. Over that time the water a field produces cools as injected water draws heat from the rock, and operators drill makeup wells to hold output.

Nevada publishes the monthly temperature of every producing geothermal well. We tracked 18 fields with ten or more years of record; ten of them, from fastest cooling to warming, show the spread:

| Field (regulator code) | Years | First-year mean | 2025 mean | Change per year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Blue Mountain (BLU) | 2009 to 2025 | 368 °F | 281 °F | -5.4 °F |
| WRS2 (WRS2) | 2015 to 2025 | 261 °F | 212 °F | -4.9 °F |
| Jersey Valley (JVP) | 2012 to 2025 | 331 °F | 292 °F | -2.9 °F |
| McGinness Hills 2 (MGH2) | 2015 to 2025 | 336 °F | 307 °F | -2.9 °F |
| Brady Hot Springs (BHS) | 2012 to 2025 | 280 °F | 248 °F | -2.5 °F |
| McGinness Hills (MGH) | 2012 to 2025 | 335 °F | 306 °F | -2.2 °F |
| Steamboat (STB) | 2012 to 2025 | 290 °F | 263 °F | -2.1 °F |
| Patua (PTA) | 2013 to 2025 | 303 °F | 293 °F | -0.8 °F |
| Dixie Valley (DXV) | 2012 to 2025 | 330 °F | 330 °F | 0.0 °F |
| Stillwater (STW) | 2009 to 2025 | 270 °F | 297 °F | +1.7 °F |

The median of all 18 fields is a change of about -1.9 °F per year. A field's mean also moves when operators add or retire wells, so these figures describe the produced water, not the rock alone. All 18 fields are in our guide [is geothermal energy renewable](https://zemanium.com/guides/is-geothermal-energy-renewable), and every yearly value is in [one JSON file](https://zemanium.com/data/nevada-field-temperature.json), CC BY 4.0.

The clearest single well-pair record is Fervo's Project Red, which went from 347 °F at its 2024 plateau to 316 °F in July 2026. Our [Project Red tracker](https://zemanium.com/fervo-project-red) scores a forecast of it, registered on 19 November 2026, against the regulator's record every month.

05 / Integrity

## What fails first in a geothermal well.

The steel and cement. A well heats when it produces and cools when cold water is pumped in or the well is shut in, and each cycle stresses the casing and its couplings. A 2018 review of 20 high-temperature wells found that most well failures came from thermal stress during quenching or the start of production. Iceland's IDDP-2 had its production casing damaged between 2,307 and 2,380 m, presumably by repeated heating and cooling. Downhole electronics stop working near 210 to 225 °C.

That is our field. We rebuilt IDDP-1's production casing in a model and ran it through the well's recorded history, and we are building Pandora, a casing joint for wells at 450 to 500 °C. The [superhot rock guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/superhot-rock-geothermal) has the record and the sources.

06 / Heat pumps

## Geothermal heat pump wells are a different thing.

A home or office geothermal heat pump uses the steady temperature a few hundred feet down; it makes no electricity. For a vertical system, holes about 4 inches across are drilled about 20 feet apart and 100 to 400 feet deep, according to the US Department of Energy. The shallowest power well in the table above goes more than 20 times deeper.

07 / Questions

## Common questions.

### How deep is a geothermal well?

For power plants, typically 1.5 to 2.5 km for conventional hydrothermal sites and 3 to 7 km for deep enhanced geothermal, by the NLR baseline. Recent wells range from 9,000 feet at The Geysers to 19,448 feet of measured depth at Fervo's Sawtooth 7 in Utah. Heat pump boreholes are 100 to 400 feet.

### How much does a geothermal well cost?

Fervo Energy reported its Cape Station wells falling from $9.4 million to $4.8 million each. NLR's analysis puts those wells at $346 to $634 per foot drilled, and drilling at 30% to 57% of a new geothermal plant's capital cost.

### How long does a geothermal well last?

Wells and plants run for decades; NLR's baseline assumes 30 years, and The Geysers has produced since 1960. The water they produce cools over time: the median long-running Nevada field ran about 1.9 °F cooler each year, and operators add makeup wells to hold output.

### How long does it take to drill a geothermal well?

Weeks. The fastest of Fervo's first six Cape Station wells took 20 days for 13,289 feet, down from 58 to 72 days for its Project Red pilot wells, and the company reported 19,448 feet in 21 days in 2026. The Geysers GDC-36 well took 69 days for 9,000 feet.

### How hot is the water in a geothermal well?

Power plants use water or steam at 300 to 700 °F, according to the EIA. Cape Station's production test ran at about 195 °C (383 °F), and research wells in Iceland have met fluid above 400 °C.

Guide · [Toni Zemani](https://zemanium.com/about#toni-zemani) · 24 November 2026

# Is geothermal energy renewable? What the field records show.

Yes. Geothermal energy is renewable because the Earth keeps producing heat inside it, as the US Energy Information Administration puts it. A single reservoir can still cool when a plant draws heat faster than the rock refills it, and Nevada's public well records show how fast that happens, field by field.

Field temperatures and plant output are measured and operator-reported to the Nevada Division of Minerals. Flow-weighted means are computed by Zemanium from that record.

01 / Answer

## Is geothermal energy renewable or nonrenewable?

Geothermal energy is renewable. The heat comes from the Earth's interior, which keeps producing it, and power plants send the used water back underground. The EIA classes it as a renewable source on that basis.

The heat in one reservoir refills slowly, over decades to centuries. So a field can be renewable as a resource while a given well pair cools during its working life. Operators manage that with spacing, injection and new wells.

02 / Mechanism

## How does geothermal energy work?

1. Wells reach hot water or hot rock deep underground.
2. Hot water or steam rises to the surface and drives a turbine, directly or through a second fluid in a binary plant.
3. The cooled water goes back down an injection well and heats up again in the rock.

Because nothing burns and the loop runs in any weather, a geothermal plant delivers power around the clock. The three plant types, dry steam, flash and binary, are explained in our [guide to geothermal power plants](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-power-plants). [Enhanced geothermal systems](https://zemanium.com/guides/enhanced-geothermal-systems) build the same loop in hot rock that has no natural water or cracks.

03 / Record

## What Nevada's field records show.

Nevada publishes the monthly temperature of every producing geothermal well. Across 18 fields with ten or more years of record and production in 2025, the flow-weighted mean temperature fell by more than 5 °F in 11, stayed within 5 °F in 3 and rose in 4. Statewide geothermal output was 5,044 GWh in 2019 and 5,031 GWh in 2025.

| Field (regulator code) | First year | First-year mean | 2025 mean | Change |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Blue Mountain (BLU) | 2009 | 368 °F | 281 °F | -87 °F |
| WRS2 (WRS2) | 2015 | 261 °F | 212 °F | -49 °F |
| Jersey Valley (JVP) | 2012 | 331 °F | 292 °F | -38 °F |
| WRS (WRS) | 2013 | 260 °F | 227 °F | -32 °F |
| Brady Hot Springs (BHS) | 2012 | 280 °F | 248 °F | -32 °F |
| McGinness Hills 2 (MGH2) | 2015 | 336 °F | 307 °F | -29 °F |
| McGinness Hills (MGH) | 2012 | 335 °F | 306 °F | -29 °F |
| Tuscarora (TUS) | 2012 | 341 °F | 313 °F | -28 °F |
| Salt Wells (SWL) | 2009 | 276 °F | 248 °F | -28 °F |
| Steamboat (STB) | 2012 | 290 °F | 263 °F | -27 °F |
| Patua (PTA) | 2013 | 303 °F | 293 °F | -10 °F |
| Soda Lake (SDL) | 2012 | 329 °F | 325 °F | -4 °F |
| Dixie Valley (DXV) | 2012 | 330 °F | 330 °F | -1 °F |
| Wabuska (WAB) | 2012 | 209 °F | 209 °F | +0 °F |
| Desert Peak (DPK) | 2012 | 295 °F | 302 °F | +7 °F |
| San Emidio (SEM) | 2012 | 284 °F | 300 °F | +16 °F |
| Stillwater (STW) | 2009 | 270 °F | 297 °F | +27 °F |
| Beowawe (BEO) | 2012 | 274 °F | 324 °F | +50 °F |

A field's mean also moves when operators add or retire wells, so this table shows the produced fluid, not the rock alone. The yearly values for every field are in [one JSON file](https://zemanium.com/data/nevada-field-temperature.json), CC BY 4.0.

The clearest single well-pair record is Fervo's Project Red, which went from a 347 °F plateau in 2024 to 316 °F in July 2026. [See the monthly tracker](https://zemanium.com/fervo-project-red).

04 / Practice

## How operators keep a geothermal field hot.

- **Reinjection.** Sending the used water back keeps reservoir pressure up and returns the fluid for reheating. Most plants reinject, according to the EIA.
- **Well spacing.** Injection wells placed far enough from producers give the water more rock to heat it before it returns.
- **Makeup wells.** When a well cools, operators drill a new one into hotter rock nearby.
- **Even flow.** In enhanced systems, spreading flow across many fractures uses more rock and slows cooling. Our [reservoir explorer](https://zemanium.com/demo/) shows the effect.

05 / Trade-offs

## Geothermal energy pros and cons.

| Pros | Cons |
|---|---|
| Runs day and night in any weather | Good conventional sites are limited to hot regions |
| About 99% less carbon dioxide than fossil plants, per the EIA | Drilling is expensive and dominates the cost |
| Most plants send their water back underground, per the EIA | Single reservoirs can cool over a plant's life |
| Fuel cost is zero | Stimulation can trigger small earthquakes |

Our [cost guide](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-electricity-cost) shows what geothermal electricity costs per megawatt-hour and which inputs move it.

06 / Questions

## Common questions.

### Why is geothermal energy considered renewable?

Because the Earth keeps producing heat in its interior, and power plants return the used water underground to be heated again. The US Energy Information Administration lists geothermal as a renewable energy source.

### Can a geothermal reservoir run out?

A reservoir can cool if heat is drawn out faster than the surrounding rock replaces it. In Nevada's records, 11 of 18 long-running fields produced cooler fluid in 2025 than in their first recorded year, and operators drill makeup wells to hold output.

### Is geothermal energy clean?

Geothermal plants burn no fuel. The EIA reports about 97% less sulfur compounds and about 99% less carbon dioxide than fossil fuel plants, and plants use scrubbers to remove hydrogen sulfide.

### How long does a geothermal power plant last?

Plants commonly run for decades, with wells replaced or added as fields cool. Our cost model assumes a 25-year life for a new plant.

07 / Sources

## Sources.

1. US Energy Information Administration, [Geothermal explained](https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/geothermal/), read 24 November 2026.
2. US Energy Information Administration, [Geothermal energy and the environment](https://www.eia.gov/energyexplained/geothermal/geothermal-energy-and-the-environment.php), read 24 November 2026.
3. Nevada Division of Minerals, [Geothermal Production and Well Data](https://data-ndom.opendata.arcgis.com/pages/oilgasandgeothermalproduction), workbook of 29 September 2026. Measured, operator-reported.

Guide · [Toni Zemani](https://zemanium.com/about#toni-zemani) · 20 November 2026

# Superhot rock geothermal: what happens above 375 °C.

Superhot rock geothermal means producing heat from rock hotter than about 375 °C at pressures above 22 MPa. Water there is supercritical, and the US Department of Energy says it can deliver several times the power density of cooler rock. Two research wells in Iceland have met fluid hotter than 400 °C, and both were damaged.

Every figure below is quoted from the source listed beside it. Targets are labelled as targets.

01 / In brief

## The short answer.

- The threshold is the critical point of water, about 374 °C and 22.1 MPa. ARPA-E and the US Department of Energy both define superhot as above 375 °C.
- ARPA-E expects a superhot well to produce up to 30 to 50 megawatts of electricity, against about 10 for an enhanced geothermal well today.
- Iceland's IDDP-1 well flowed steam at 450 °C and suffered acid corrosion and silica erosion. IDDP-2 logged 426 °C at about 4,550 m and its casing was damaged.
- Wells fail through their steel, cement and instruments. Casing breaks when the well is heated and cooled, and electronics stop working near 225 °C.

02 / Motive

## Why go hotter.

Each well is expensive, so power per well drives the price of electricity. ARPA-E says current equipment holds enhanced geothermal to about 220 °C and about 10 megawatts of electricity per production well, and that superhot reservoirs could raise this to 30 to 50. Its SUPERHOT program aims at 10 to 20 GW of baseload power at under $30 per megawatt-hour by 2040.

Other estimates of output per well exist. A 2022 study by LucidCatalyst and HERO for the Clean Air Task Force modelled 17 to 29 MW per production well at 55 kg/s. Iceland's power company Orkuveitan is targeting 20 to 50 MW from one well in the IDDP-3 project, and says it has not demonstrated that figure. Conventional wells there make 2 to 7 MW.

03 / Record

## Wells drilled so far.

| Well | What was measured | What went wrong |
|---|---|---|
| IDDP-1, Krafla, Iceland | superheated steam at 450 °C and 140 bar at the wellhead | condensed steam carried hydrochloric and hydrofluoric acid; silica eroded surface equipment when wellhead pressure fell below 80 bar; repeated shutdowns increased corrosion |
| IDDP-2, Reykjanes, Iceland | 426 °C at 340 bar logged at about 4,550 m; about 600 °C inferred at the bottom | production casing damaged between 2,307 and 2,380 m, presumably by cyclic heating and cooling |
| Newberry, Oregon (Mazama Energy) | 331 °C in October 2025; a later well above 700 °F | none reported |

At IDDP-2 the logging tools stayed below 65 °C in rock hotter than 400 to 500 °C for as long as cold water circulated. The production casing was damaged all the same, presumably by repeated heating and cooling.

Next in line: IDDP-3 in Iceland is planned in four stages from late 2026 to 2028. Quaise Energy's Project Obsidian in Oregon targets a well above 400 °C and first power in 2030. Quaise drills with millimetre waves and had completed a 118 m hole in granite by July 2025.

04 / Limits

## What fails first.

| Component | Published limit | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Casing and couplings | most well failures in a review of 20 high-temperature wells came from thermal stress during quenching or the start of production | Kruszewski and Wittig, 2018 |
| Portland cement with 35% to 40% silica flour | proven where produced fluid stays below 350 °C | Kruszewski and Wittig, 2018 |
| Downhole electronics in service | about 210 to 225 °C | Hephae, 2026; IMAPS HiTEC, 2016 |
| Temperature logging tools | 350 °C for four hours | Kruszewski and Wittig, 2018 |
| Polyimide-coated optical fibre | 300 °C continuously, 350 °C briefly | manufacturer's statement (Exail) |
| Silicon carbide circuits, in the laboratory | one year at 500 °C in air | NASA Glenn, 2018 |
| Casing connection test standard ISO/TS 12835:2022 | written for wells that cycle from well below 180 °C up to maxima of 180 °C to 350 °C or above; covers connections only | ISO |

ARPA-E's program description says conventional steel casing and Portland cement are inadequate for superhot wells, and that well materials have to survive high temperature, rapid temperature change and corrosive fluid for 15 years or more.

05 / Funding

## Who is funding it.

- ARPA-E SUPERHOT announced eight awards on 12 November 2026: Blade Energy Partners ($6.3m), Lawrence Livermore ($5.5m), Los Alamos ($3.5m), University of Oklahoma ($3.1m), Oak Ridge ($3.0m), University of Southern California ($3.0m), XGS Energy ($3.0m) and Pacific Northwest National Laboratory ($2.6m).
- The US Department of Energy is funding a superhot EGS demonstration above 375 °C on the western flank of Newberry Volcano in Oregon.
- Japan's NEDO plans five 100 MW class supercritical geothermal plants around 2040 to 2050 and estimates the resource at 11 GW.
- The European SHiFT consortium received €10m from Horizon Europe for technology above 400 °C.
- Mazama Energy raised $135m in September 2026. Quaise Energy closed a Series B of $180m in August 2026.

06 / Zemanium

## What we are working on.

Our work is on the well itself: how casing and cement behave through heating and cooling cycles above 375 °C, and how to record a test so that someone outside the company can check it. We use gauges that can be bought today. In November 2026 we stopped our own long-line acoustic sensor after it failed a simulation gate we had set in advance; the [record is on the research page](https://zemanium.com/room/#sensing).

We rebuilt IDDP-1's production casing in a model and ran it through the well's recorded history: two discharges, then the kill of July 2012. The video log of 2014 found three couplings pulled apart at 300, 356 and 505 m. In 88 of 128 sampled wells our model reproduces that log (SIMULATED, registered and time-stamped before the run). The string parts first at 292 m, just below the point at 290 m where the outer anchor casing changes size, with gaps inside the logged 250 to 400 mm. Two wellhead readings the model was never fitted to land inside their measured bands. The model is calibrated to one well, and the next run is aimed at the second and third partings.

That replay is the test bench for Pandora, our casing joint for wells at 450 to 500 °C. Pandora is built to carry a string through the same history without parting. Its first metal, a subscale joint, is next.

If you operate, design or finance hot wells and want to compare notes, write to [toni@zemanium.com](mailto:toni@zemanium.com).

07 / Questions

## Common questions.

### What is superhot rock geothermal?

It is geothermal energy from rock hotter than about 375 °C at pressure above 22 MPa, where water becomes supercritical. A well in those conditions can carry several times the energy of a conventional geothermal well.

### How hot is superhot rock?

Above 375 °C by the definitions of ARPA-E and the US Department of Energy. Iceland's IDDP-1 produced steam at 450 °C, and IDDP-2 logged 426 °C with about 600 °C inferred at the bottom of the well.

### Has anyone produced power from superhot rock?

No commercial plant runs on superhot rock yet. IDDP-1 flowed steam at 450 °C and IDDP-2 logged 426 °C at 340 bar, and both wells were damaged. Quaise Energy targets first power in Oregon in 2030, and Japan's NEDO plans plants around 2040 to 2050.

### What is the IDDP?

The Iceland Deep Drilling Project, a research programme run by Icelandic energy companies to drill into supercritical geothermal zones. IDDP-1 was drilled at Krafla, IDDP-2 at Reykjanes, and IDDP-3 is planned from late 2026.

### Why do superhot wells fail?

Mostly from thermal cycling. Steel casing expands when the well heats and contracts when cold water is pumped in, and the stress breaks casing and couplings. A 2018 review of 20 high-temperature wells found that most failures came from thermal stress during quenching or the start of production.

### How much power can one superhot well produce?

ARPA-E expects up to 30 to 50 megawatts of electricity per well, compared with about 10 megawatts for an enhanced geothermal well at 220 °C. That output has not been demonstrated.

Tool · [Toni Zemani](https://zemanium.com/about#toni-zemani) · 27 November 2026

# LCOE calculator: the levelized cost of energy of any power plant.

Enter what a plant costs to build and run, how much it produces and how long it lasts, and the calculator returns its levelized cost of energy (LCOE) in dollars per megawatt-hour. It uses the simple formula the US national laboratories publish, and starts on a new geothermal plant built to Lazard's 2026 assumptions: $91.11 per megawatt-hour.

Presets are midpoints of the low and high inputs in Lazard's Levelized Cost of Energy+ version 19.0 (July 2026). The calculator leaves out taxes, depreciation and cost escalation, so its results sit near Lazard's published ranges without matching them exactly.

01 / Calculator

## Calculate LCOE. Start from Geothermal, new plant (Lazard 2026 midpoint) Solar PV, utility scale (Lazard 2026 midpoint) Wind, onshore (Lazard 2026 midpoint) Gas combined cycle (Lazard 2026 midpoint) Nuclear (Lazard 2026 midpoint) Your own numbers Capital cost, $ per kW Fixed operating cost, $ per kW per year Variable operating cost, $ per MWh Fuel cost, $ per MWh Capacity factor, % Own use of output (pumps, auxiliaries), % Life, years Discount rate (cost of capital), % Plant size, MW Levelized cost of energy $91.11 per MWh

Capital share

$72.15

Fixed operating share

$0.00

Change any field and the result updates. Plant size changes the totals, not the cost per megawatt-hour.

The calculator needs JavaScript. The formula below gives the same result by hand.

For geothermal plants with a simulated reservoir behind them, our [power-cost model](https://zemanium.com/confidence/) runs 1,080 scenarios on GEOPHIRES-X output and shows how the price moves with well cost, plant cost and the cost of money.

02 / Meaning

## What is LCOE?

The levelized cost of energy (LCOE), also called the levelized cost of electricity, is the constant price per megawatt-hour at which a power plant earns back everything spent on it over its life, including the return its lenders and owners expect. It puts plants with very different cost structures on one scale: a solar farm that is cheap to build and produces a quarter of the time, a geothermal plant that is expensive to drill and runs day and night, and a gas plant that is cheap to build and pays for fuel every hour.

03 / Formula

## The LCOE formula.

The full definition discounts every year's cost and every year's output back to today:

`LCOE = sum over years t of (capital + operating + fuel cost in year t) / (1 + r)^t, divided by sum over years t of (electricity in year t) / (1 + r)^t`

When the plant is built at once and costs and output are the same each year, that reduces to the simple form the National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR, formerly NREL) publishes, which this calculator uses:

`LCOE = (capital cost per kW x CRF + fixed O&M per kW-year) x 1000 / (8760 x capacity factor) + variable O&M + fuel cost`

`CRF = r (1 + r)^n / ((1 + r)^n - 1)`

Here `r` is the discount rate, `n` the life in years and CRF the capital recovery factor, the share of the capital cost that has to be recovered each year. The factor 1000 turns kilowatts into megawatts and 8760 is the number of hours in a year.

04 / Worked example

## How to calculate LCOE, step by step.

A new geothermal plant on Lazard's 2026 midpoint inputs: $5,885 per kW to build, $15.125 per kW-year fixed and $16.925 per MWh variable operating cost, no fuel, an 85% capacity factor, a 25-year life and a 7.7% discount rate.

1. Capital recovery factor: 0.077 x 1.077^25 / (1.077^25 - 1) = 0.0913.
2. Yearly cost per kW: $5,885 x 0.09129 + $15.125 = $552.37.
3. Yearly output per kW: 8,760 hours x 85% = 7,446 kWh, or 7.446 MWh.
4. Fixed cost per MWh: $552.37 / 7.446 = $74.18.
5. Add variable cost and fuel: $74.18 + $16.925 + $0 = $91.11 per MWh.

The same plant costs $69.55 per MWh at a 4% discount rate and $106.03 at 10%. Almost all of a geothermal plant's cost is paid before it runs, so the cost of money moves its price more than any operating figure. Our [guide to geothermal electricity cost](https://zemanium.com/guides/geothermal-electricity-cost) shows what sets each input.

05 / Comparison

## LCOE by energy source in 2026.

| Technology | Unsubsidized LCOE, $/MWh | Average | Capital cost, $/kW | Capacity factor |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Onshore wind | $37 to $99 | $68 | $1,900 to $2,750 | 30% to 55% |
| Solar PV, utility scale | $40 to $98 | $69 | $1,250 to $1,850 | 20% to 30% |
| Geothermal | $67 to $111 | $89 | $5,135 to $6,635 | 80% to 90% |
| Gas combined cycle | $51 to $129 | $90 | $1,450 to $2,100 | 30% to 90% |
| Coal | $72 to $177 | $125 | $3,495 to $7,405 | 65% to 85% |
| Offshore wind | $105 to $167 | $136 | $5,600 to $7,100 | 45% to 55% |
| Gas peaking | $144 to $276 | $210 | $1,100 to $1,650 | 10% to 15% |
| Nuclear | $175 to $255 | $215 | $12,300 to $17,570 | 89% to 94% |

Source: Lazard, Levelized Cost of Energy+ version 19.0, July 2026, new-build plants in the United States without tax credits.

06 / Limits

## What LCOE leaves out.

- When the power arrives. A megawatt-hour at 7 pm on a still winter evening is worth more to a grid than one at noon in spring. Lazard publishes a separate cost of firming intermittency for that reason.
- Grid costs. Transmission, interconnection and balancing sit outside the LCOE of a single plant.
- Output that changes with age. The simple formula assumes the same output every year. A geothermal reservoir can cool and a solar panel degrades; the full discounted formula takes a year-by-year output instead.
- Risk. Exploration wells that miss, construction overruns and fuel price swings shift the real cost. Our [power-cost model](https://zemanium.com/confidence/) draws 2,000 combinations of them.

07 / Questions

## Common questions.

### What does LCOE stand for?

Levelized cost of energy, or levelized cost of electricity. It is the price per megawatt-hour at which a power plant exactly pays back its lifetime costs, including the return on the money invested.

### How do you calculate LCOE?

Multiply the capital cost per kilowatt by the capital recovery factor, add the fixed operating cost per kilowatt-year, divide by the megawatt-hours each kilowatt produces in a year (8.76 times the capacity factor), then add variable operating and fuel cost per megawatt-hour.

### How do I calculate LCOE in Excel?

The capital recovery factor is =PMT(rate, years, -1), for example =PMT(0.077, 25, -1) returns 0.0913. Then LCOE = (capex_per_kW * CRF + fixed_OM) * 1000 / (8760 * capacity_factor) + variable_OM + fuel.

### What is a good LCOE?

It depends on what the plant delivers. In Lazard's 2026 figures new onshore wind and utility solar average $68 and $69 per megawatt-hour, geothermal $89 and gas combined cycle $90. Geothermal and gas run when needed; wind and solar need storage or backup for that.

### What is the LCOE of geothermal energy?

Lazard puts new geothermal at $67 to $111 per megawatt-hour in 2026, average $89. Public US geothermal power contracts signed from 2019 to mid-2025 priced at $67.50 to $99. The US Department of Energy targets $45 for enhanced geothermal by 2035.

### Is this LCOE calculator free?

Yes. It runs in your browser, needs no account and stores nothing. The text and tables on this page are CC BY 4.0, and the calculator code is MIT licensed.

2. National Laboratory of the Rockies, [Simple Levelized Cost of Energy (LCOE) Calculator Documentation](https://nlr.gov/analysis/tech-lcoe-documentation), read 27 November 2026 (formula).

03 / Hardware

## Hardware drawings.

These are development drawings of engineering geometry. Release for hot service is decided by physical test campaigns at the matching duty.

- [SL-D01-A release demonstrator, dimensioned build sheet](https://zemanium.com/assets/hardware/SL-D01-A-build-sheet.svg). Room temperature, 56 mm of gate travel.
- [Release demonstrator, exploded view](https://zemanium.com/assets/hardware/shiftlatch-demo_exploded.svg), with [held](https://zemanium.com/assets/hardware/shiftlatch-demo_held.svg) and [released](https://zemanium.com/assets/hardware/shiftlatch-demo_released.svg) states.
- [E7-SPC-B specimen kit, build sheet](https://zemanium.com/assets/hardware/E7-SPC-B-kit-build-sheet.svg).
- [Sliding seal cassette, cutaway](https://zemanium.com/assets/hardware/thermoslip-cassette-cutaway.svg).
- [Thermal test bench, general arrangement](https://zemanium.com/assets/hardware/heatmux-thermal_verification_general-arrangement-preview.png).

The [research page](https://zemanium.com/room/#machines) shows each drawing with its development record.

05 / Licence

## What you may do with it.

| Material | Licence | In practice |
|---|---|---|
| Guides, page text, charts and simulation records | [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) | Copy, quote, translate and build on it, commercially or otherwise, if you credit Zemanium and link the page. |
| Code in the pages and models | [MIT](https://opensource.org/license/mit) | Use it in your own software and keep the copyright notice. |
| Hardware drawings | Published for review, all rights reserved | Read them, check them, cite them. To manufacture from them or use them commercially, ask us for a licence. |
| Utah FORGE data | CC BY 4.0, from its authors | Credit SLB, the University of Utah and Utah FORGE as the source record does. |
| The Zemanium name and logo | Not licensed | Use the name to refer to us. |

Copyright 2026 Toni Zemani.

06 / Citation

## How to cite.

For a guide: Toni Zemani, title of the guide, Zemanium, date shown on the page, and its address. For a model or record: Zemanium, name of the item, its date, its address, and the label it carries (SIMULATED).

Example: Zemanium, "Power-cost model", 5 October 2026, https://zemanium.com/confidence/. SIMULATED.

07 / Agents

## For software agents.

[llms.txt](https://zemanium.com/llms.txt) lists every page with a one-line description. [llms-full.txt](https://zemanium.com/llms-full.txt) holds the guides in one Markdown file. Each guide also has a Markdown copy at its own address with `.md` added. The [sitemap](https://zemanium.com/sitemap.xml) lists canonical addresses. Search and AI crawlers are allowed on the whole site, and the same files are mirrored at [github.com/tonizemani2/zemanium-open](https://github.com/tonizemani2/zemanium-open).

08 / Contact

## Work with us.

We publish so that specialists can check the work, and so that people with a problem we can help with can find us. Three kinds of conversation have a clear next step.

| You have | We can |
|---|---|
| A forecast, cost case or test plan you need checked | Review it independently and give you the numbers we reproduce and the ones we cannot |
| A well, tool or material problem above 200 °C | Scope a sponsored experiment with a fixed question, a named engineer and raw results at the end |
| A use for one of the hardware designs | License it, or develop it with you |

Write to [toni@zemanium.com](mailto:toni@zemanium.com) with what you need to decide. Investors and engineers who want to join are welcome at the same address.
